column1: p0_l00|2.1|0.77|It is the spring of 1718.
p0_l01|8.1|0.95|you are 23 years old, a sailor on a merchant ship off the coast of the Carolinas and a black flag has just appeared on the horizon.
p0_l02|5.3|1.00|In about two hours, someone is going to offer you a choice that will decide the rest of your life.
p0_l03|2.3|1.00|you probably think you know what comes next.
p0_l04|0.9|0.00|eyepatches.
p0_l06|1.0|1.00|walking the plank.
p0_l07|1.2|1.00|buried treasure.
p0_l08|1.6|1.00|Almost none of that is true.
p0_l09|5.4|1.00|The real life of a pirate was stranger, in some ways fairer and much, much shorter.
p0_l10|3.1|1.00|So let's live it from the day you join to the day it ends.
p1_l00|4.1|1.00|The pirate ship is faster than yours, and it has far more men on deck.
p1_l01|5.5|1.00|Your captain looks at the flag, looks at the guns, and does what most merchant captains did.
p1_l02|1.6|1.00|He surrenders without a fight.
p1_l03|2.4|1.00|That was the whole point of the black flag.
p1_l04|3.0|1.00|It said, give up now and nobody gets hurt.
p1_l05|2.1|1.00|Resist and expect no mercy.
p1_l06|2.4|1.00|Pirates wanted cargo, not battles.
p1_l07|3.4|1.00|A battle could damage the prize and kill their own crew.
p1_l08|1.5|1.00|so the pirates come aboard.
p1_l09|5.7|0.92|They take food, sales, rope, tools, medicine, alcohol, and anything they can sell.
p1_l10|2.5|1.00|Then they turn to your crew and ask a question.
p1_l11|1.3|1.00|Who wants to join us?
p1_l12|1.7|1.00|Why would anyone say yes?
p1_l13|1.1|1.00|Look at your life.
p1_l14|7.2|1.00|A sailor's wage is small, the food is bad, the work is brutal, and a captain can have you flogged for talking back.
p1_l15|5.8|1.00|Some pirates were forced to join, usually carpenters and surgeons, because their skills were valuable.
p1_l16|2.0|1.00|but many sailors volunteered.
p1_l17|1.1|1.00|you step forward.
p1_l18|1.4|1.00|and they hand you a piece of paper.
p2_l00|5.5|1.00|Every pirate crew had a written contract called the articles and every man signed it or made his mark.
p2_l01|2.6|1.00|They read like a strange early democracy.
p2_l02|3.1|1.00|The crew elects the captain, and the crew can vote him out.
p2_l03|2.1|1.00|in a fight his word is law.
p2_l04|2.8|1.00|The rest of the time, big decisions go to a vote.
p2_l05|6.7|1.00|The crew also elects a quartermaster who keeps order and divides the loot so the captain cannot simply take it.
p2_l06|2.6|1.00|and the loot is split surprisingly fairly.
p2_l07|8.2|1.00|On Bartholomew Roberts' ship, the captain and quartermaster got two shares. A few officers got one and a half and everyone else got one.
p2_l08|3.2|1.00|On a merchant ship, the owners kept almost everything.
p2_l09|1.8|1.00|there was even a kind of insurance.
p2_l10|5.0|0.83|Under the buccaneer Henry Morgan, losing a right arm paid 600 pieces of 8.
p2_l13|1.2|1.00|and there were rules.
p2_l14|5.0|0.93|Roberts's articles banned gambling for money on board and ordered lights out at eight o'clock.

p2_l15|12.8|0.95|Another cruise article said that anyone caught stealing from his shipmates or trying to desert could be marooned, left alone on an island with a bottle of water, a bottle of gunpowder, a pistol and some shot.
p3_l00|2.3|1.00|So what is daily life actually like?
p3_l01|1.7|1.00|First, it is crowded.
p3_l02|9.5|0.92|A ship that 20 merchant sailors would run might carry 100 pirates or more, because pirates needed lots of men to board prizes and to sail the ships they captured.
p3_l03|2.2|1.00|You sleep wherever you can find space.
p3_l04|4.9|1.00|You eat ship's biscuit so hard you soak it before biting and often full of weevils.
p3_l05|4.8|1.00|You eat salted meat that has been sitting in a barrel for months, and turtle when you can catch one.
p3_l06|4.7|1.00|Fresh water goes bad in the casks, so you drink whatever alcohol you have captured.
p3_l07|3.1|1.00|Every few months, the whole ship has to be careened.
p3_l08|9.8|1.00|You sail into a hidden cove, haul her onto the beach, tip her on her side, and scrape the hull clean of weed, barnacles and shipworms, which can eat right through the planks.
p3_l09|3.7|1.00|For those days, the ship cannot run and cannot fight.
p3_l10|2.4|1.00|and the real danger is not the Navy.
p3_l11|5.8|1.00|Like every sailor of your time, you are far more likely to die of disease than in battle.
p3_l12|2.9|1.00|scurvy, tropical fevers, infected wounds.
p3_l13|1.5|1.00|A small cut can kill you.
p4_l00|1.4|1.00|What about the famous stuff?
p4_l01|4.6|1.00|Walking the plank, there is almost no evidence that Pirates of Your Era did it.
p4_l02|2.2|1.00|it shows up mostly in later stories.
p4_l03|1.9|1.00|buried treasure, very rare.
p4_l04|4.3|1.00|Pirates spent their money fast on drink, gambling, and good times in port.
p4_l05|10.3|0.91|The most famous case, Captain Kidd, buried some of his loot on Gardner's Island near New York in 1699, and it was dug up within weeks and used as evidence against him.
p4_l06|6.0|0.87|eye patches and parrots mostly come from fiction, especially Treasure Island, published in 1883.
p4_l07|2.4|1.00|and the loot itself is rarely gold.
p4_l08|10.0|1.00|A typical prize carries cloth, sugar, tobacco, timber, tools, and sometimes enslaved people. A dark part of this history that the movies leave out.
p4_l09|3.7|1.00|Sometimes the most valuable thing on board is the ship itself.
p4_l10|6.6|0.90|In May 1718, Blackbeard blockaded the port of Charleston with several ships and took hostages.
p4_l11|2.0|1.00|And what did he demand as ransom?
p4_l12|1.4|1.00|a chest of medicine.
p5_l00|2.0|1.00|between raids, where do you go?
p5_l01|4.1|0.84|In 1718 the answer is Nassau in the Bahamas.
p5_l02|3.3|1.00|For a few years it is a pirate base with no real government.
p5_l03|9.2|0.96|Hundreds of pirates, a harbor too shallow for big warships to follow you in, a beach lined with tents and taverns where captured goods are sold and drunk.
p5_l04|4.2|1.00|Blackbeard, Charles Vane and Calico, Jack Rackham all pass through.
p5_l05|3.5|0.82|but in the summer of 1718, everything changes.
p5_l06|6.7|0.95|Britain sends a new governor, a former privateer named Wood Rogers, with warships and an offer from the king.
p5_l07|3.7|1.00|any pirate who surrenders will be pardoned for everything he has done.
p5_l08|1.4|1.00|Hundreds take the pardon
p5_l09|3.2|1.00|Some of them go straight back to piracy within months.
p5_l10|4.2|1.00|Rogers even sends former pirates out to hunt down their old friends.
p5_l11|2.0|1.00|And now you have your second big choice.
p5_l12|3.4|1.00|Take the pardon, settle down, and hope nobody remembers you.
p5_l13|1.1|1.00|or keep sailing.
p6_l00|1.2|1.00|Let's say you keep sailing.
p6_l01|2.0|1.00|Here is how it usually ends.
p6_l02|3.6|1.00|Most pirate careers in this era lasted only a year or two.
p6_l03|7.6|0.93|Even the most successful pirate of all, Bartholomew Roberts, who took more than 400 ships, lasted less than four years.
p6_l04|2.6|0.75|He was killed in battle in 1722.
p6_l05|7.2|0.92|Blackbeard was killed in November 1718 in a brutal fight with a Royal Navy crew off North Carolina.
p6_l06|4.6|0.94|It was said he had been shot five times and cut about 20 times before he fell.
p6_l07|3.6|0.86|Calico Jack was captured in 1720 and hanged in Jamaica.
p6_l08|7.3|0.92|Two of his crew, Anne Bonney and Mary Reed, were sentenced to hang as well, but escaped the rope by announcing that they were pregnant.
p6_l09|4.8|1.00|If you are captured, there is a trial and it almost always ends the same way.
p6_l10|7.4|1.00|In London, pirates were hanged at execution dock on the Thames, and their bodies left until three tides had washed over them.
p6_l11|5.7|0.86|After Robert's crew was captured, 52 of them were hanged in a single trial in West Africa.
p7_l00|1.2|1.00|So, was it worth it?
p7_l01|9.0|1.00|For men who had been flogged and underpaid on merchant and navy ships, piracy offered something they had never had, an elected captain, a fair share, a vote.
p7_l02|1.6|1.00|In a twisted way it was freedom.
p7_l03|2.6|1.00|but the price was a life measured in months.
p7_l04|4.6|0.82|By about 1726, the golden age of piracy was over.
p7_l05|6.0|1.00|Navies hunted the pirates down, colonies stopped buying their loot, and pardons and hangings did the rest.
p7_l06|2.9|1.00|thousands of men sailed under the black flag.
p7_l07|3.1|1.00|Very few got rich, and almost none grew old.
p7_l08|3.8|0.87|and yet 300 years later, kids still dress up as them.
p7_l09|2.5|0.82|So go back to that morning in 1718.
p7_l10|3.9|1.00|the black flag on the horizon, the quartermaster asking his question.
p7_l11|0.8|1.00|Would you sign?
p7_l12|1.4|1.00|Tell me in the comments.
p7_l13|6.1|1.00|And if you want to find out what your life would be like as a Roman legionary, subscribe because that is next.
